video_title: Dino Mavrookas: America Needs to Build Ships Again
transcript: The US used unmanned sea drones for the first time during a recent attack in Iran, and a company here in Austin created those drones. Saronic is a defense tech company that focuses on creating boat-like sea drones for the military. >> Not just the defense market, [music] but the entire maritime industry is centered around autonomy. That's what we're building for at Saronic. We're actually [music] going to be able to launch a hypersonic missile off of the back of Marauder, which is an autonomous ship, before the Navy completes their first test of a hypersonic missile off of a manned vessel. >> That's crazy. >> If we ever actually do get into a conflict in [music] Taiwan Strait that leads to World War III or anything dramatic, China can outproduce the rest of the world in terms of ships. China outbuilt the US 230 to 1. And the [music] naval fleet that we have today is actually shrinking. They built over a thousand commercial ships last year. The United States built five. [music] >> One last question. It's the most difficult question. >> Okay. >> Some people had to walk out of the room because I asked this question. >> I won't walk out on you. >> [laughter] >> What is your hottest take right now? >> [music] >> Dino, welcome back. This is your second trip. We recently just went into your facility, looked at all the Corsairs, and we just saw a Mirage, and now we're here in uh I don't know. What do you call this space? >> This is This is our all-hands space. This is where we bring the team together. We hold fun events. We shot our Christmas party here. I think we had over a thousand people at our last Christmas party. >> Wow. >> So, this is a a collaborative area where folks can come together, work in a really casual space, bring the production team together with the engineering team, um and just make sure that we continuously are collaborating and just sharing information across the company. >> To set the table, we talked a bit about your stats when we started the last walking tour, and if you haven't watched it, you should watch it. But so, you're now at over a $9 billion valuation. You raised $2.6 billion. You've just announced This was a little debate. Is it still going to be fresher a month? I think so. But Port Alpha, $3 billion Port Alpha. So, I guess to bring all of that to focus against the backdrop of what's going on in America, I'd love for you to lay out kind of the stats that we're working with. Palantir CTO Shyam just talked about this, but we're ratioed by China in shipbuilding. >> It's actually pretty crazy. So, China outbuilds the US 230 to 1. Um the naval fleet that we have today is actually shrinking. So, there's right around 290 ships in in our naval fleet. In 2018, Congress actually set a statutory minimum of 355 ships. That was 8 years ago. Um and we're going in the wrong direction. In 2024, the Navy actually looked at it and said, "Oh, we don't actually need 355. We need 381." And these are just manned ships, let alone all the unmanned ships that we're going to need in our fleet. And the shipbuilding infrastructure that we have in this country today just won't won't support that. That's why we started Saronic. That's why we started building autonomy. That's why we flipped focus so heavily on production and manufacturing. Not just of Corsair and Mirage, which we saw earlier, but of Marauder and now of Port Alpha, much larger ships. How do we start actually building both defense and you know, like large defense and large commercial ships in this country again? >> I want to talk a little bit about the bureauc- the bureaucracy and what's kind of like entangled there. >> [laughter] >> Where are we going to start? >> I know. But so so in that clip of Shyam, he was talking about how bureaucracy has just clogged up the system. And so much so that it resulted to this. So, what is kind of the state of that? I mean, we just we just had Rob on and he was talking about uh acquisition reform. >> Yeah, well, he he leads that up for for us front and center every single day. He's dealing with our with the Navy customer. And what I will say is I I kind of give two sides of it. One, there has been movement, right? I I was in the SEAL Teams for 11 years, 2004 to 2015. Well, the last 5 years were on SEAL Team Six. Again, that this is the fastest I've actually seen the government move with with anything. So, there is a lot of urgency around it. The new administration is putting a lot of focus in this area. You see the president's budget request for $1.5 trillion. They put out a maritime executive order and the maritime action plan specifically around shipbuilding. You have the SHIPS Act, which is in Congress, which is focused on obviously the shipbuilding industry. So, there's a lot of focus on defense, defense technology, the industrial base, and shipbuilding. And things are changing. But when you look at the budget today, let's just look at the Department of War's budget. We talked about the request for $1.5 trillion and where the budget is today, right around a trillion dollars for '26. 1% 1% went towards autonomy. So, that that's just gives you a sense of how far we actually have to go. And in terms of the bureaucracy and what needs to change, you're getting a lot of push from the top down, from leadership, from the administration, which I just highlighted, from Capitol Hill to invest in things that are not only much more economical, but also scalable. And when you talk about ships, one of the one of the biggest examples is aircraft carriers, right? They take over 10 years to make one. And then that number increases by the day, actually, because the program is just later and later and later, and the cost keeps going up and up and up. I was actually quoting $13 billion for an aircraft carrier, and I was at an event where the president spoke just last week, and he quoted $19 billion. I was like, "What is happening to the budget here?" So, you have a a lot of focus from Congress because Look, there's a 30-year shipbuilding plan in the Navy right now. We talked about going from 290 to 381 over 30 years. That'll cost $1.2 trillion if we can even execute as a country in the first place on that plan. Um what we're building at Saronic will not only provide more capabilities faster, but it'll save the taxpayer hundreds of billions of dollars by driving down costs as well. >> You talked a little bit about this on our walk, but how do you create the path that scale? >> You do it incrementally, right? And so, we we've demonstrated success at each step, and then we've went after larger and larger problems. And what we've had to do is what we've done is really bring together a world-class team, capital to invest in that team, and this again goes back to the credit to the customer where if the customer didn't move alongside us with these early wins, we wouldn't have been able to have those, right? Um we talked about Corsair and the large contract that we that we announced in December of '25, multi-hundred million-dollar contract with the Navy. If the customer didn't prioritize that, if they didn't say, "We're going to move to rapid acquisition. We're going to launch this solicitation through DIU because we need this capability, and we're just going to move fast." We wouldn't have been able to build it, but we wouldn't have been able to build the track record of success, raise more capital, invest in the next thing, which let us go and build Marauder, right? And everything we're building here is because we're investing private capital ahead of demand, ahead of need, building to scale to make sure that our warfighters get the best capability in their hands as fast as possible. And that's you mentioned Rob talked about defense acquisition reform. That's exactly what the Secretary of War is calling for. Calling for companies to invest their own capital in really big ways, build for speed and scale. That's what the department needs. That's That's his words, not mine. And that's what we're building for here at Saronic. >> Why do you think it's so prescient for the private sector to be doing this? >> It's an all of country effort, right? In order to break through the bureaucracy that you mentioned, you know, you need companies to just go and do it. You need companies like Saronic and then Anduril was before us and you know, then before that you had Palantir and SpaceX to just go and build things, to show the government that there's a different way, there's a better way. Let's not focus on cost-plus contracting and large exquisite systems and everything else. And look, before we started building Saronic, it was just a focus on, you know, big large navy ships. And I'm not I'm not saying that we don't need cruisers and destroyers and aircraft carriers and there certainly is a role for the traditional fleet and there should be investment into the legacy industrial defense industrial base as it stands because we we need the primes that exist today. We just need other companies to be built alongside of them to support in the platforms that they're not able to build and the technology that they're not able to build um to really benefit and make sure that the US remains the most powerful military in the world. >> Drew Odney actually gave a couple great questions and one of them was how many new primes do you think there will be? >> I don't know the answer to that. >> Right? >> No, I mean you don't know. There's not probably not going to be a hundred, right? When you look back, even if you go back to 1993, I think the number is 55 or 60 or somewhere in there. And that 55 or 60 went down to five, right? Over the course of 20 or 30 years as the department kind of shrunk its base and it enforced consolidation. And now we're in the reversal of that trend. Do I think we get all the way up to 55? I mean, it just depends on your definition of prime. Prime just means a company that is contracting directly with the government not through another company as a subcontractor. And so, I mean, I'll define prime as directing contracting directly with the government at some sort of large scale. I think over the next five to 10 years, I'll I'll answer. I won't dodge the question completely. I think there will be somewhere around five to 10. I think you'll see five to 10 really like big impactful companies scale over the next five to 10 years. And hopefully more. >> And how are you thinking about dual use in your commercial strategy? >> So, this is something that I I actually think it's overlooked a little bit is the importance of commercial when providing capabilities to Department of War. Um especially in shipbuilding. The commercial shipbuilding builds the supply chain and builds the industrial base. It lets you build for scale so that you're not only reliant on naval orders, which are bespoke orders and low volume. That's the first step into how this shipbuilding fiasco even started was the commercial shipbuilding industry kind of went away and the supply chain and the workforce went with it. If you're going to to advantage of economies of scale, if you're going to build robust and resilient supply chains, you need a commercial strategy. With even Corsair's dual use, right? Very commercial focused. We're looking at everything from port and harbor security and operations with the Coast Guard and things outside of the traditional military sense. And then as you get into larger vessels, Marauder starts actually enabling some sort of like commercial logistics operations. And with Port Alpha, we're going to be looking at how do we bring autonomy into the commercial shipping industry at large for container ships and tankers and roll-on/roll-off vessels. This lets you build a commercial revenue base, but also is actually absolutely critical for national security. Cuz if we don't have tankers, if we don't have roll-on/roll-off vessels, it means we actually don't have the ships to resupply our force if we're actually in a conflict or a war. It's not who can build the most exquisite, the most expensive, whose ships have the most on them in terms of payloads and weapons and all the other things. It's like who can just build the most?
